title: Before you start
note: Seven questions since 2026-11-05: two screening questions (q1, q2: a course on bandits or reinforcement learning, or being able to explain an algorithm such as UCB, flag the session excluded) and the five knowledge items of set C1 (k1, k2: the maths the lesson builds on; r1 to r3: everyday statistical reasoning behind the post-test). The statistics-course question (q3) and the harder set C2 are in stash/pretest.json. One set since 2026-11-05 (C1): the pretest isn't tied to the test form, and the harder C2 was there to calibrate items in the pilot; its items are marked off, kept. The team's pretest, option C (2 November 2026): about 4 minutes before the lesson, without the rules. Three screening questions (q1 and q2 flag a session as excluded: an RL course or bandits covered in a course; could explain an algorithm such as UCB; q3, a probability or statistics course, is only recorded until the team decides), then a set of five knowledge items, each with "I don't know" and no written reason: two on the maths the lesson builds on (K1, K2: √n, ln(t)) and three on everyday statistical reasoning behind the post-test (R1 to R3: small samples scatter more, picking the best result picks up luck, you only learn about what you choose), with no algorithm named. Set C1 is the default (keys c, d, b, c, a). Set C2 measures the same five things with harder items (H1 to H5, keys c, a, b, d, c; pair names the C1 item). Pilot (settings, pretest.both): every session takes both sets, one after the other, in an order that alternates with the session's test form (A: C1 first, B: C2 first). It checks that the groups start alike and gives a covariate; it does not measure learning gain.

items.prompt: Have you taken a course on reinforcement learning, or covered multi-armed bandits in any course?
Before today, how well did you know multi-armed bandits?
options: I had never heard of them
I knew roughly how they work
I could explain an algorithm such as UCB
items.note: The team's proposal: (c) is recorded, (d) is excluded.

items.prompt: You estimate the true average of a noisy measurement twice, once from 10 readings and once from 1,000 readings. Compared with the 95% confidence interval from 1,000 readings, how wide is the interval from 10 readings?
diagnosis: the width does not depend on the number of readings
width proportional to the number of readings
items.explain: The width shrinks with √n, and √(1,000 / 10) = 10. With only 10 readings the t-value makes it about 11 times, still closest to (c). It underlies why the bonus of a rarely tried option is large and shrinks with every try (F10).

items.prompt: A quantity equals ln(t). As t goes from 10 to 100, it rises by about 2.3. How much further must t grow for the quantity to rise by another 2.3?
diagnosis: logarithm confused with a curve that levels off
equal steps in t give equal rises
the needed step doubles each time
items.explain: ln(1,000) − ln(100) = ln(10) ≈ 2.3, so each equal rise needs t to grow tenfold. It underlies why an unpicked option's bonus keeps growing without limit but takes ever longer to grow by the same amount (F11; V4, T9).

items.measures: small samples land at both ends
items.prompt: A country ranks its 1,000 schools by this year's average exam score. Schools have between 20 and 2,000 students. Suppose all schools teach equally well, so a school's average differs only because of which students happen to attend. The top 50 schools turn out to be mostly small schools. Which schools most likely make up the bottom 50?
options: Schools of all sizes, in proportion to how common they are
diagnosis: if the small ones top the list, the large ones must be at the bottom
size cannot matter when teaching is equal
the two ends of the size range take the two ends of the ranking
items.explain: Averages of small groups scatter more, so small schools fill both ends of the ranking (Wainer's "most dangerous equation"). It underlies why an early average from few tries can be far off in either direction.
items.note: In simulation (200 rankings, equal teaching, sizes 20 to 2,000), 99% of the bottom 50 were smaller than the median school. Replaces the café version of the hospital problem, which many statistics students know.

items.measures: picking the best result picks up luck
items.prompt: A company tries 20 new suppliers with one delivery each. The suppliers truly differ in quality, and each delivery's quality also varies by chance. The company gives a second order to the supplier whose first delivery was best. What should it expect from that second delivery?
options: As good as the first delivery
Worse than the first, still above the average supplier
Worse than the first, and below the average supplier
diagnosis: one result shows the true quality
a good start means a good streak
items.explain: The best first delivery was partly luck, so the second is expected to fall back towards the supplier's true quality, which is still likely above average (regression to the mean). It underlies why a too-high start corrects itself once the option is tried again (D1).

items.measures: you only learn about what you choose
items.prompt: A bank grants loans only to applicants its scoring rule rates as safe, and records whether each loan is repaid. Can the bank find out from these records whether its rule turns away many people who would have repaid?
options: No, not from these records alone
Yes, once it has enough records
Yes, if it also records the rejected applicants' incomes
diagnosis: the records cover everyone who matters
more information about them replaces their outcomes
items.explain: Rejected applicants never produce a repayment record, so no amount of data about the accepted ones, or about the rejected ones' incomes, shows how many of the rejected would have repaid. In bandit terms, an option that is never chosen never produces data (F2, F5).
